messages.content: I want to design a session-typed language that supports endpoint delegation and structured cancellation without leaving peers stranded or breaking protocol guarantees. How would you frame the goal?

The goal is to make delegation and cancellation work together within a session-typed language. Delegation must allow an endpoint to change hands without losing track of its protocol obligations. Structured cancellation must let an interaction stop without leaving a peer waiting indefinitely because the cancellation was not accounted for. The language should retain its protocol guarantees in both situations.
What does endpoint delegation add to the problem?

An endpoint carries the obligations of one side of a protocol. Delegation means another participant can take responsibility for that endpoint. The design therefore has to preserve a coherent account of who may use it and what protocol actions remain, even when responsibility moves. That is the general concern; the goal does not prescribe a particular delegation rule or implementation.
And why is cancellation more than simply stopping the participant that requests it?

A session involves peers whose next actions may depend on one another. If one participant stops while another remains waiting for an action that will never occur, the cancellation has stranded that peer. Structured cancellation is meant to make stopping an interaction compatible with the protocol discipline, rather than treating it as an untracked escape from that discipline.
So the design cannot treat delegation and cancellation as unrelated features?

Right. The goal specifically concerns delegation-and-cancellation programs. An endpoint may have changed hands when cancellation becomes relevant, so a satisfactory design needs an account of the remaining obligations that still makes sense after delegation. That does not dictate how the language represents those obligations; it identifies the interaction the design must handle.
What are the guarantees I should state explicitly?

State two requirements: establish protocol safety and cancellation progress under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery. Protocol safety concerns preserving the permitted communication behavior of sessions. Cancellation progress concerns avoiding a cancellation-related state in which peers are left stranded. Both claims should be expressed with the scheduling and delivery assumptions attached, rather than as unconditional guarantees.
Can you clarify what protocol safety means here without choosing the language's rules yet?

At this level, it means that well-formed use of the language does not break the protocol guarantees that session typing is meant to provide. Delegating an endpoint should not turn its remaining obligations into arbitrary communication, and cancellation should not make an otherwise forbidden protocol behavior acceptable. The precise formal statement belongs to the eventual design; the goal specifies what kind of guarantee must be established.
What should I be careful not to imply by saying cancellation progress?

It should not be read as a promise that every computation terminates or that progress holds regardless of the execution environment. The stated requirement is cancellation progress under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery. Its focus is that cancellation does not strand peers, not a general termination claim for all programs.
Why call out fair scheduling?

Because a progress claim needs to distinguish a participant that cannot proceed from one that could proceed but is never given a chance to run. Fair scheduling supplies an assumption about opportunities to take available steps. It is part of the conditions for the requested progress guarantee, not a claim that the language controls every scheduler.
And what work is reliable asynchronous delivery doing in that condition?

It says delivery is asynchronous while also ruling out message loss in the assumed setting. A participant need not receive a message immediately merely because it was sent. Conversely, a progress argument about communication should not have to account for messages disappearing. Neither reliability nor fairness, as stated here, supplies a numerical time bound.
I also want a concrete acceptance criterion. What is it?

Under separate compilation, the language should accept 12 valid delegation-and-cancellation programs and reject 12 protocol-invalid variants. Those are two distinct requirements: acceptance of the 12 valid programs and rejection of the 12 protocol-invalid variants. They are goals for the design, not results already demonstrated.
Does separate compilation matter to both sides of that criterion?

Yes. The requirement is stated under separate compilation for both acceptance and rejection. It is not enough to handle the valid programs only when everything is examined as one undivided unit, or to identify protocol-invalid variants only under that condition. The design must support those outcomes in the separate-compilation setting.
Should I assume that each invalid variant is paired with exactly one of the valid programs?

No exact pairing is specified. The stated numbers are 12 valid delegation-and-cancellation programs to accept and 12 protocol-invalid variants to reject. Calling them variants identifies their role in the rejection criterion, but it does not supply a one-to-one mapping or the contents of either collection.
Does rejecting the invalid variants mean rejecting programs for any possible reason?

The requirement is specifically to reject the 12 protocol-invalid variants. Its point is to distinguish violations of the session protocol from valid delegation-and-cancellation uses. It does not enumerate other kinds of invalidity or set a separate target for them.
How do the numerical criterion and the safety and progress requirement relate?

They assess different aspects of the same design goal. Protocol safety and cancellation progress are guarantees to establish under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery. Accepting 12 valid programs and rejecting 12 protocol-invalid variants under separate compilation is a concrete discrimination requirement. Meeting a collection of examples alone would not, by itself, state the general safety and progress guarantees.
Would it be fair to say that accepting valid delegation programs is insufficient if cancellation can still leave a peer waiting?

Yes. The goal requires support for delegation and structured cancellation without stranded peers or broken protocol guarantees. Merely allowing an endpoint to be delegated would not address what happens to its peers when cancellation matters. The design has to account for both features and their interaction.
Likewise, could a cancellation scheme avoid stranded peers yet still be unsuitable if it compromises the protocol?

Yes. Avoiding a stranded peer does not excuse violating protocol safety. The two concerns are concurrent requirements: cancellation must make progress under the stated assumptions, and communication must retain its protocol guarantees. A design that addresses one while breaking the other would not meet the stated goal.
Can I already specify how cancellation is propagated or how delegated endpoints are tracked?

The goal does not settle those design choices. You can identify the obligations they would have to satisfy, but choosing a particular propagation mechanism or endpoint-tracking representation would add a decision not present here. The current target is the combination of features, guarantees, assumptions, and separate-compilation acceptance and rejection requirements.
What would be a concise way to keep the scope of the claim honest?

You could say: design a session-typed language with endpoint delegation and structured cancellation; establish protocol safety and cancellation progress, without stranded peers, under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery; and, under separate compilation, accept 12 valid delegation-and-cancellation programs while rejecting 12 protocol-invalid variants. That states the intended guarantees and criterion without suggesting they have already been met.
What design direction would bring endpoint delegation and structured cancellation together?

A proposal is to combine affine delegation, cancel-labelled session transitions, and acknowledged scope-wide cancellation over ownership graphs. For separate compilation, the proposal also calls for publishing effect-annotated interfaces. These are connected parts of one design direction, not guarantees that the design has already been validated.
What does “affine delegation” contribute?

An affine discipline limits an endpoint’s use to at most one use rather than allowing it to be copied and used independently in multiple places. Applied to delegation, it offers a way to transfer the ability to use an endpoint without treating both the sender and recipient as free to continue using it. That matters because the remaining session obligations need a coherent holder after delegation.
Does affine mean an endpoint can simply be dropped whenever it is inconvenient?

No. Affineness alone is not a complete cancellation policy. Even if an ownership discipline permits an endpoint to cease being used locally, an unaccounted-for drop could leave its peer waiting. The proposal pairs affine delegation with explicit cancellation-related protocol transitions and scope-wide cancellation rather than relying on affineness by itself to protect peers.
What are cancel-labelled session transitions supposed to express?

They make cancellation visible in the session-transition account. Instead of treating cancellation as an event outside the protocol, the proposal gives it a labelled place in the account of how a session can move from one state to another. The node does not specify the transition rules or say that cancellation is permitted at every protocol state.
Why does the label matter if cancellation is handled at the scope level too?

The two ideas address different aspects of the same concern. Cancel-labelled transitions address how cancellation relates to a session’s protocol state. Scope-wide cancellation addresses how cancellation reaches the relevant participants when obligations extend across a scope. Without the protocol-facing part, a scope mechanism alone would not explain how session guarantees are retained.
Could I describe a cancel-labelled transition as just another ordinary message?

That would go beyond what is specified. The proposal says the transitions are cancel-labelled, but it does not settle whether the label corresponds to an ordinary message, a distinct runtime event, or some other representation. The important point here is that cancellation is accounted for in the session transitions.
What does “scope-wide” rule out?

It rules out thinking of cancellation solely as one endpoint’s isolated decision to stop while all related obligations are ignored. The proposal treats cancellation as applying across a relevant scope. It does not yet define the boundary of every scope or the exact procedure for bringing participants within it into the cancellation process.
And what makes the cancellation “acknowledged”?

The proposal includes acknowledgments as part of scope-wide cancellation, so cancellation is not described merely as a signal sent with no account of its reception or handling. It does not specify who acknowledges what, the precise ordering of acknowledgments, or the condition under which a scope is considered finished. Those would need definition in the language design.
I do not want “acknowledged” to sound like normal protocol completion.

It need not. An acknowledgment of cancellation can be understood as part of accounting for cancellation, not as a claim that the session completed its ordinary path. Keeping those notions distinct helps preserve the meaning of protocol guarantees while still addressing the risk of stranded peers.
How do ownership graphs fit into scope-wide cancellation?

An ownership graph is the proposed way to reason about which obligations and participants are connected through endpoint ownership. That is especially relevant when delegation moves responsibility for an endpoint. Cancellation over such graphs aims to account for the relevant scope rather than relying only on whoever currently holds one local endpoint.
Are you saying the graph has a particular set of node and edge types?

No. The proposal names ownership graphs but does not give their formal representation. A design would have to define what an ownership relationship means and how delegation is reflected in that account. Specifying particular node or edge types now would add detail not present in the proposal.
Is the graph meant to solve protocol safety by itself?

No single component is presented as a complete solution. Affine delegation addresses how endpoint use is transferred; cancel-labelled transitions address cancellation in the protocol account; acknowledged scope-wide cancellation over ownership graphs addresses the connected obligations; and effect-annotated interfaces support reasoning across compilation boundaries. Protocol safety and cancellation progress would still need to be established for the combined design.
Can you explain the interaction when an endpoint has been delegated, without inventing a specific runtime algorithm?

Conceptually, delegation changes who is responsible for the endpoint’s remaining protocol actions. If cancellation later concerns that endpoint, a scope-wide account needs to follow the relevant ownership relationships rather than assume the original holder is still responsible. The proposal expresses that intention through affine delegation and ownership graphs, while leaving the operational details open.
What should the proposal say about a peer that might otherwise wait indefinitely?

That is the risk the structured cancellation part is intended to address. A cancel-labelled protocol account and acknowledged cancellation across the relevant scope are proposed so that stopping one part of an interaction does not silently strand a peer. The proposal does not itself prove that this outcome is achieved; cancellation progress remains something to establish under the stated fair-scheduling and reliable-asynchronous-delivery assumptions.
Why not rely on the ownership graph and omit the cancel labels?

The graph and the labels serve different purposes in the proposal. The graph concerns the reach of ownership-related obligations, while cancel-labelled transitions concern the protocol meaning of cancellation. Knowing who may be affected does not by itself say how a session changes state when cancellation occurs.
And why not keep the cancel-labelled transitions but omit the acknowledgments?

A protocol transition can describe that cancellation is recognized as a possible kind of change, but that description alone does not account for cancellation across a scope of connected participants. The acknowledgment aspect is proposed to make the scope-wide handling explicit. The precise acknowledgment requirement remains unspecified.
Where do effect-annotated interfaces enter the picture?

They are the proposed interface information for separate compilation. Publishing an effect-annotated interface would let another compilation unit see relevant effect information without relying on access to the implementation body. This connects the delegation-and-cancellation design to the separate-compilation requirement, while leaving the exact effect vocabulary and interface format undecided.
Does “publish” mean making a public document, or something more technical?

Here it can be read as making the annotated interface available at a compilation boundary. The proposal does not specify a publication channel or file format. The essential point is that effect information is exposed for separate compilation rather than remaining available only inside the implementation.
Can we already say which effects the annotations list?

Not exactly. The proposal calls them effect-annotated interfaces in a design centered on delegation and cancellation, but it does not enumerate the annotations or their formal meanings. It would be reasonable to ask how an interface conveys information relevant to those features; claiming a particular effect set would be an additional design choice.
Why is interface information important if session types already describe communication?

The proposal suggests that the information needed at a separate-compilation boundary is not being left entirely implicit in an implementation. Session types concern protocol behavior, while effect annotations would expose relevant effects through an interface. Exactly how those two forms of information relate is part of the design to work out, not a relationship fixed by this proposal alone.
Would separate compilation still require a coherent view of delegated obligations?

Yes, as a design concern. Compiling components separately should not make endpoint delegation or cancellation invisible to the checks needed across their boundary. The proposal’s answer is to publish effect-annotated interfaces; whether a particular interface system supplies enough information would need to be shown.
I want to avoid implying that the 12 valid programs have already been accepted and the 12 protocol-invalid variants rejected.

Then keep the proposal and its evaluation criterion separate. The proposed combination describes what to build. Acceptance of 12 valid delegation-and-cancellation programs and rejection of 12 protocol-invalid variants under separate compilation remain requirements to assess, not reported results of this proposal.
Likewise, the proposal is not yet a proof of safety or progress?

Correct. It identifies mechanisms intended to support protocol safety and cancellation progress. Establishing those properties under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery requires an actual account of the language and its behavior. Naming affine delegation, cancel-labelled transitions, ownership graphs, acknowledgments, and annotated interfaces does not itself establish the properties.
Is there a compact way to state the proposal without turning open details into decisions?

Propose a session-typed design that combines affine delegation with cancel-labelled session transitions and acknowledged, scope-wide cancellation over ownership graphs, and publishes effect-annotated interfaces for separate compilation. That states the components and how they are grouped without specifying an unchosen graph representation, acknowledgment protocol, transition rule, or interface syntax.
There is still a race I cannot pin down: when cancellation occurs while delegation is in flight, which owner must acknowledge the peer’s cancel transition before the scope can close?

That is an open question in the proposal. Affine delegation is meant to keep endpoint responsibility from being duplicated, but an in-flight transfer makes it necessary to say when that responsibility changes hands. Without that rule, the proposal does not identify whether the delegating owner, the receiving owner, or an owner determined by some specified transfer point must acknowledge the peer’s cancel transition before scope closure.
Why does the transfer being in flight make the acknowledgment ambiguous?

Because sending an endpoint and having its recipient take responsibility for it need not be treated as the same event in an asynchronous setting. If cancellation overlaps that interval, referring simply to “the owner” may not identify who is responsible for acknowledging the peer’s cancel transition. The design needs an unambiguous account of ownership for this case; it has not yet supplied one.
Could I just say the owner at the instant cancellation starts must acknowledge?

You could investigate that as a possible rule, but the proposal does not adopt it. It would also require defining what counts as the instant cancellation starts relative to an in-flight delegation. Otherwise, the phrase moves the ambiguity from “which owner” to “which event determines ownership.”
What if I instead mean the owner when the cancel transition is observed?

That is another possible way to identify a responsible owner, not an answer already fixed by the proposal. You would have to say whose observation matters and how it relates to the transfer of the endpoint. With asynchronous delivery, different participants need not observe relevant events at the same time.
Is the core issue whether the original holder or the recipient has the obligation?

Yes. The question asks which owner is responsible for acknowledging the peer’s cancel transition when delegation and cancellation overlap. Calling one party the original holder and the other the recipient makes the alternatives easier to discuss, but their roles alone do not settle the obligation. The design must specify how responsibility changes during delegation.
Could both acknowledge it?

That is a possible question to examine, but it is not the rule stated here. Requiring both would be different from requiring acknowledgment by whichever party owns the endpoint at a defined point. The design would need to explain why any chosen acknowledgment condition matches its affine ownership discipline and when that condition permits the scope to close.
Does affineness itself force exactly one of them to send the acknowledgment?

No such conclusion follows from the proposal alone. Affineness concerns limiting endpoint use rather than freely duplicating it. It does not, by itself, specify the timing of a transfer in flight or assign the acknowledgment obligation for a concurrent cancel transition.
I want to be precise about what is being acknowledged. Is it the delegation?

The question is specifically about acknowledging the peer’s cancel transition before the scope can close. Delegation creates the ownership uncertainty, but the acknowledgment at issue concerns cancellation. Treating it merely as confirmation that delegation happened would change the question.
Nor should I assume that acknowledging cancellation means the ordinary session finished?

Correct. The acknowledgment under discussion belongs to scope-wide cancellation. It should not be silently equated with completion of the session’s ordinary protocol path. The question is whether the appropriate owner has accounted for the peer’s cancel transition so that closing the cancellation scope is justified.
How does this relate to the ownership graph?

The ownership graph is the proposed account of relationships affected by delegation and scope-wide cancellation. For this race, it would need to represent or otherwise determine which ownership obligation remains relevant while the endpoint is being transferred. Merely invoking the graph does not answer which owner must acknowledge; that depends on rules the proposal has not specified.
Can reliable asynchronous delivery settle who owns the endpoint?

No. Reliable asynchronous delivery is an assumption about delivery, not a rule for transferring ownership. It does not make sending and receipt simultaneous, or choose who must acknowledge a cancel transition that overlaps delegation.
Would fair scheduling resolve the race eventually?

Fair scheduling concerns opportunities to take enabled steps. It cannot decide which party has the acknowledgment obligation if the language has not assigned that obligation. The progress requirement relies on fair scheduling, but the ownership question still needs a semantic answer.
Could scope closure simply wait until someone acknowledges, without specifying who?

That would leave the central question unanswered. If an acknowledgment from an unrelated or no-longer-responsible participant sufficed, the condition might not account for the peer’s cancel transition. Conversely, if no participant could determine that it was responsible, closure might remain blocked. The proposal needs to identify the relevant owner, or otherwise specify an equally precise responsibility condition, before treating acknowledgment as a closure condition.
Is the danger specifically that each side assumes the other owns the obligation?

That is one way the ambiguity could matter: neither the delegating party nor the recipient would act if each treated acknowledgment as the other’s responsibility. A different mismatch could arise if an acknowledgment were accepted without establishing that it came from the party responsible under the ownership rules. These illustrate why the rule matters; they are not reported behaviors of a defined language.
Does the cancel-labelled transition already tell us who acknowledges it?

Not as stated. A cancel label makes cancellation part of the session-transition account, but the proposal does not specify an ownership rule for a transition racing with delegation. It also does not define the acknowledgment procedure. Those descriptions have to be connected before the scope-closing question has a determinate answer.
How should I phrase the unresolved point without proposing an accidental solution?

Ask which owner, under the language’s ownership-transfer rules, must acknowledge the peer’s cancel transition when cancellation races with an in-flight delegation, and make clear that the acknowledgment is required before the scope closes. That preserves the race and the closure condition without choosing the original holder, the recipient, or a particular transfer point.
Should the question also distinguish an endpoint being sent from ownership having transferred?

Yes, that distinction explains why the race needs attention. You need not assume a particular moment at which ownership transfers; you can leave that as part of what the design must clarify. Otherwise, saying “current owner” risks hiding the very uncertainty the question raises.
So what can we say now about closing the scope?

Only that the question makes acknowledgment of the peer’s cancel transition by the appropriate owner a condition to resolve before scope closure. The proposal has not yet defined which owner is appropriate in the in-flight delegation case, so it does not yet supply a definite scope-closing rule for that race.
I have a hypothesis for the delegation race: assign cancellation responsibility to the sender until transfer acknowledgement, and then to the receiver. Could that prevent missing acknowledgements?

That is the proposed hypothesis. It gives the responsibility for acknowledging cancellation an explicit handoff point: the sender remains responsible until transfer acknowledgement, after which the receiver is responsible. The intended benefit is to prevent the peer’s cancel transition from going unacknowledged when cancellation races with delegation. That benefit still needs to be established; the rule is not yet a proven guarantee.
Why use transfer acknowledgement as the boundary rather than the act of sending the endpoint?

Sending the endpoint is precisely where an in-flight interval can begin. If the sender ceased to be responsible immediately on sending, the proposed account could leave uncertainty about who must handle cancellation before the transfer is acknowledged. Keeping responsibility with the sender until transfer acknowledgement is meant to avoid that gap. This explains the hypothesis; it does not yet prove that the rule covers every execution.
Does this mean the receiver has no cancellation responsibility before transfer acknowledgement?

Under this proposed assignment, the sender retains that responsibility until transfer acknowledgement. The receiver takes it afterward. That statement is about who owes the relevant cancellation acknowledgement; it does not, by itself, specify everything either participant may do with the endpoint while delegation is in flight.
What if the peer’s cancel transition happens while the delegation is still in flight?

The hypothesis assigns responsibility to the sender so long as transfer acknowledgement has not occurred. Once it has occurred, responsibility belongs to the receiver. For a race, the design would have to define those events precisely enough to apply that boundary to the peer’s cancel transition.
So I should not just say that whichever participant notices cancellation first acknowledges it?

Not if you mean to express this hypothesis. It assigns responsibility according to transfer acknowledgement, not according to which participant happens to notice cancellation first. In an asynchronous setting, observations may occur at different times, so substituting a first-observer rule would be a different proposal.
Am I talking about the same acknowledgement in both parts of the sentence?

No. Transfer acknowledgement marks the proposed change in cancellation responsibility from sender to receiver. The acknowledgement the rule is meant to keep from going missing concerns the peer’s cancel transition. Acknowledging the transfer does not, merely by being an acknowledgement, acknowledge cancellation.
Would the sender still be responsible if the endpoint has been sent but the transfer has not been acknowledged?

Yes, that is the central boundary in the hypothesis: responsibility stays with the sender until transfer acknowledgement. The act of sending alone does not move cancellation responsibility under this proposed rule.
And after transfer acknowledgement, is it definitely the receiver rather than the original sender?

That is what the hypothesis assigns: after transfer acknowledgement, cancellation responsibility belongs to the receiver. Whether this assignment prevents missing acknowledgements in all delegation races remains a claim to examine, not an established result.
Why is the handoff relevant to closing the cancellation scope?

The open issue is which owner must acknowledge the peer’s cancel transition before the scope can close. The hypothesis offers a candidate answer to the ownership part: sender until transfer acknowledgement, receiver afterward. Scope closure still depends on the appropriate cancellation acknowledgement; the transfer acknowledgement alone should not be mistaken for that condition.
Could I conclude that the scope can close as soon as the transfer is acknowledged?

No. Transfer acknowledgement only marks the proposed shift in who bears cancellation responsibility. It does not establish that the peer’s cancel transition has been acknowledged. Those are distinct matters, and the question about closing the scope concerns the latter.
What does the word “prevents” commit me to in this hypothesis?

It states the outcome the rule is expected to deliver: no missing cancellation acknowledgements during delegation races. Because the node is a hypothesis, that outcome should be presented as what the assignment is proposed to prevent, not as an observed or proven result.
Could I phrase it as a guarantee under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery already?

Not yet. Those are the stated assumptions for the broader cancellation-progress requirement, but they do not themselves establish this particular hypothesis. A guarantee would require a defined account of the transfer acknowledgement, cancellation responsibility, and their interaction in the race, followed by an argument that acknowledgements cannot be missed.
Does affineness settle that argument for us?

No. Affine delegation motivates keeping endpoint responsibility coherent, but affineness alone does not establish the timing of this cancellation-responsibility handoff or show that the peer’s cancel transition is always acknowledged. The proposed sender-to-receiver assignment supplies a candidate rule whose consequences still need examination.
Is this hypothesis saying that both parties should acknowledge cancellation during the handoff?

No. It assigns responsibility to the sender until transfer acknowledgement, then to the receiver. It does not propose a period in which both are required to acknowledge the same cancel transition. Nor does it specify the detailed procedure for an acknowledgement that overlaps the handoff.
Could the ownership graph simply label the sender as responsible before that boundary and the receiver afterward?

That is a conceptual way to relate the hypothesis to ownership graphs: the responsibility tracked by the design would follow the proposed handoff. The node does not prescribe a graph representation or an update procedure, so it is better to describe the before-and-after responsibility than to commit to particular graph operations.
I want to distinguish an acknowledgement getting delayed from one going missing. Does the hypothesis do that?

Its claimed benefit concerns missing acknowledgements during delegation races. It does not set a time bound for acknowledgement, and reliable asynchronous delivery does not make delivery instantaneous. A delayed acknowledgement and an obligation that nobody has taken responsibility for are different concerns; the hypothesis targets the latter by proposing a continuous assignment of responsibility.
What if the sender and receiver disagree about whether transfer acknowledgement has happened?

That identifies a detail the hypothesis would need to make precise. The phrase “until transfer acknowledgement, then the receiver” needs a defined event or condition that can determine the handoff despite the race. The hypothesis supplies the proposed boundary, but not the full operational account of how participants learn or apply it.
Can I say that the rule avoids every possible problem caused by concurrent delegation and cancellation?

No. Its stated claim is narrower: assigning cancellation responsibility to the sender until transfer acknowledgement and then to the receiver is hypothesized to prevent missing acknowledgements during delegation races. It does not claim to resolve every concurrency issue or establish all protocol guarantees on its own.
What is the most careful one-sentence version?

Hypothesis: keeping cancellation responsibility with the sender until transfer acknowledgement, then assigning it to the receiver, prevents the peer’s cancel transition from missing an acknowledgement when cancellation races with delegation.
How should we turn the question about cancellation racing with delegation into a concrete plan?

Specify ownership handoff rules, model-check delegation races, and prove that each cancel acknowledgement has exactly one responsible owner. The handoff rules would make responsibility precise; model checking would examine race behavior under those rules; and the proof would address the general ownership claim. These are planned steps, not completed results.
What needs to be specified in the ownership handoff rules?

They need to say when responsibility for an endpoint changes hands during delegation, including what happens while the transfer is in flight. For this question, they must also make clear which owner is responsible for a cancel acknowledgement on either side of that handoff. Otherwise, the phrase “the responsible owner” remains ambiguous at precisely the point where cancellation may race with delegation.
Should those rules just formalize the sender-until-transfer-acknowledgement idea?

That idea is a relevant candidate: the sender retains cancellation responsibility until transfer acknowledgement, and the receiver takes it afterward. The plan here is to specify ownership handoff rules and examine them; it does not by itself declare that candidate proved or settle every detail of its formalization.
Why specify the rules before model-checking the races?

A race can be examined meaningfully only if the model says what delegation and cancellation do to ownership. In particular, a check needs a defined way to determine who bears an acknowledgement obligation when events overlap. Otherwise, an apparent absence or duplication of responsibility could reflect an underspecified model rather than a property of the proposed language.
When you say “model-check delegation races,” what is the focus?

The focus is the interaction between an in-flight delegation and cancellation: whether the ownership account still identifies the party responsible for a cancel acknowledgement as the events can occur in different orders. The plan does not specify a model checker, a state bound, a particular encoding, or any findings.
Would model checking alone establish the exactly-one-owner claim?

Not by itself. Model checking can examine the delegation races represented in a model. The plan separately calls for a proof that each cancel acknowledgement has exactly one responsible owner. That proof is the proposed way to establish the ownership claim for the specified rules, rather than treating checked cases as a substitute for it.
What exactly does “exactly one” require?

It has two parts. At least one owner must be responsible for each cancel acknowledgement, so the obligation is not lost during a handoff. At most one owner must be responsible, so responsibility is not assigned ambiguously to multiple owners. Both parts matter when cancellation overlaps delegation.
Is the claim that exactly one acknowledgement is actually sent?

No. The stated proof target is that each cancel acknowledgement has exactly one responsible owner. Responsibility is an assignment of obligation. Whether an acknowledgement is actually performed, delivered, or sufficient for scope closure involves further behavioral questions; those should not be silently folded into this particular proof target.
Does “each cancel acknowledgement” refer to the transfer acknowledgement too?

No. The plan concerns cancel acknowledgements. A transfer acknowledgement, if used as a handoff boundary, concerns delegation; it is distinct from acknowledging the peer’s cancel transition. Keeping those separate is important when asking who is responsible before the cancellation scope can close.
Could an ownership rule be precise while still leaving a gap in responsibility?

Yes, precision alone would not make it the right rule. A rule might precisely identify an interval in which neither party is responsible. That would fail the “at least one” part of the proposed proof target. The plan calls for rules whose consequences can be checked and for a proof of exactly one responsible owner, not merely for an unambiguous description of a gap.
And could it assign responsibility to both sides?

It could, unless the rules exclude that possibility. Assigning both owners responsibility for the same cancel acknowledgement would fail the “at most one” part. The proof target therefore tests both missing responsibility and overlapping responsibility during a delegation race.
Does this plan answer which owner acknowledges the peer’s cancel transition before scope closure?

It is a plan to obtain a precise answer, not a report that the answer has already been established. The handoff rules would identify the owner at the relevant point; model checking would examine races; and the proof would establish that the specified account assigns exactly one responsible owner to each cancel acknowledgement. The scope-closing question motivates why that assignment matters.
What if the rules identify one owner, but the scope closes without the peer’s cancel transition being acknowledged?

Then the ownership assignment alone would not justify that closure. Proving exactly one responsible owner addresses who owes the acknowledgement, not whether a proposed scope-closing rule waits for it. The plan’s stated proof target should be kept distinct from a broader proof of cancellation progress or correct scope closure.
How does this fit with the requirement for cancellation progress under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery?

It addresses a necessary responsibility question within that broader goal: an acknowledgement obligation should not disappear or become multiply assigned during delegation. Fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery remain the stated assumptions for cancellation progress, but they cannot compensate for an ownership account that fails to say who is responsible. This plan does not itself establish the broader progress property.
Should the model-checking results be described as evidence already in hand?

No. Model-checking delegation races is a planned activity. No model, explored cases, counterexamples, or results are stated here. The same applies to the proof: the plan names what is to be proved, not a theorem that has already been proved.
Do we need to decide the exact model-checking tool or proof method in this plan?

No such choices are specified. The plan commits to specifying the ownership handoff rules, model-checking delegation races, and proving the exactly-one-responsible-owner property for cancel acknowledgements. Tool selection and the form of the proof remain open.
Would a proof about one particular race ordering be enough?

The wording “each cancel acknowledgement” calls for a general ownership claim under the specified rules, not just an explanation of a single ordering. Individual orderings may help illustrate or check the handoff, but they would not, on their own, fulfill the stated proof objective.
Can I state the plan without implying that the proposed handoff hypothesis has already passed a test?

Yes: specify ownership handoff rules for delegation, model-check races between delegation and cancellation, and prove that every cancel acknowledgement has exactly one responsible owner. That leaves the proposed handoff to be made precise and examined, without presenting a planned check or proof as a completed result.
For the delegation-race work, what exactly is the model-checking activity?

Model-check 48 two-hop delegation/cancellation interleavings in TLA+, using reliable FIFO queues, and record orphaned acknowledgements and duplicate owners. The activity examines the proposed ownership handoff under overlapping delegation and cancellation. It specifies what to check and record, not what the checks will find.
What does “two-hop” mean in this activity?

It means the cases concern delegation across two successive transfers, rather than only a single transfer. That makes it possible to examine cancellation while responsibility may be moving through more than one handoff. The activity does not specify particular participants or a particular sequence of transfers beyond that two-hop scope.
Why examine interleavings instead of describing one representative race?

The ownership question depends on the order in which delegation, cancellation, and relevant acknowledgements occur. Examining interleavings lets the model check the differing orders represented in the two-hop scenario, rather than assuming one order stands for them all. The stated count is 48 interleavings; it does not say how they are distributed among outcomes.
Does 48 mean 48 programs?

What would protocol preservation assert?

How are the two proposed proof goals related?

They constrain different aspects of execution. Protocol preservation asks whether reduction steps retain the session guarantees.
